name: Carla Olsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making the time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a business reporter for the regional daily, mostly for its weekly business section and the business pages online. I cover the port, the two big factories on the ring road, and local firms putting out results. A normal day is reading company filings in the morning, ringing a few bosses or their press people, and then going out to something like a factory opening or a chamber of commerce breakfast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the people, oddly. Business owners are more honest over coffee than people think. What wears me out is the accounts, I'm honestly not great at reading a balance sheet yet. Ines, the senior business reporter, checks my numbers and has saved me from at least two embarrassing mistakes. I use an AI tool now and then to summarise long reports, but I always check it against the real thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds about right to me. The tool I use is helpful but it's not magic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI turned out to be a useful helper, not a replacement, and businesses should stop panicking. I'd probably write a column about local firms that spent a lot on it and didn't get much back. Our readers would like that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, my job looks fine in this picture. The business section makes money from sponsors, which is more than you can say for the rest of the paper. Half my job is reading company accounts, and a tool that summarises them a bit faster just means I get to lunch on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, and get better at accounts. I'd ask Ines to go through one set of results with me every Friday. I'd keep overpaying the mortgage on my flat by about two hundred a month. And I'd keep using the summary tool, because it does save time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. My worries would be normal ones, like the mortgage rate going up when the fixed deal ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me about your cushion. How secure are you if something went wrong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought a one-bed flat last year with a small mortgage, and I've still got about seven months of pay saved. There are lots of business and finance writing jobs in the city. So I'd be okay, I'd just need to move quickly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is anything at the paper worrying you in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rest of the paper, a bit. They've cut the print run twice. But business news has sponsors, so I think we'd be the last section to go.

I'd write a column about **local firms** that spent big on AI and saw little back.
think: Privately my job looks **fine**, because the business section earns money from **sponsors**.
A faster **accounts summary** tool just means I get to lunch on time.
do: Go through **one set of results** with Ines every Friday.
Overpay the **mortgage** by about two hundred a month.
Keep using the **summary tool** and checking it.
feel: **Calm**, with ordinary worries about the **mortgage rate** when the fix ends.

fieldNote: Her section **earns its keep** through sponsors, which makes her feel secure.
She's honest about **weak accounts skills** and has a plan to improve.
She owns a **flat** and has seven months saved, a solid base for her age.

steps.text: Review one company's results with Ines every Friday
Overpay the flat mortgage by about two hundred a month
Keep using the AI summary tool on long company reports

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one makes me sit up. Writing and checking is exactly what I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say firms and newsrooms should use AI where it works and be honest about where it doesn't. I'd say it at work in a fairly calm way. I'd also say people need help retraining, but it's not the end of the world.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Quarterly results stories are the first thing to go, because a company's numbers come out at seven and a machine can write them up by five past. That's maybe a third of my week. The interviews and the coffees with bosses would stay, I think, but there'd be fewer of us doing them. Ines would be safe, and I'm not sure I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools properly once the senior people had shown they work, maybe after six months. I'd push to do more interviews and features, the human side, and fewer results stories. I'd stop overpaying the mortgage and build my cash back up to a year. And I'd start quietly talking to comms people at the port about what their jobs look like.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Not panicking, but it'd be on my mind every time a results story came in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd talk to the port's comms people. Is that a step away from journalism?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It is, and I'm not thrilled about it. But it pays well and it's still writing and people. I'd rather have a door open than not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your parents say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My dad runs a small plumbing business, so he'd say, told you, learn a trade. My mum would say stay, you love it. Neither would be much help, but both would mean well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. Gosh. That's before my fixed mortgage deal even ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say governments need a plan quickly, especially for young people who've just started careers. I'd say businesses should slow down cuts until there's support in place. I'd say it in a measured way, I'm not one for shouting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I bought my flat last year assuming I'd be a reporter for thirty years, and in this picture I'd be lucky to get three. It's all thinking work, my job, so it goes in 2028. Even the port comms job would go then. The only parts that last longer are physically being somewhere, and nobody pays a business reporter just to stand in a factory.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd build cash to fifteen months of costs straight away, cutting holidays and eating out. I'd look hard at whether to sell the flat or rent it out, so I'm not stuck with a mortgage and no job. I'd talk to my dad about the plumbing business, honestly, because hands-on work has three more years. And I'd wait a little to see what the government offers before signing up for any course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Not panicked, I've got savings, but it'd keep me awake.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you really join your dad's plumbing business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe the office side first, he's useless at invoices. But that's thinking work too, so it would go in 2028. I'd probably end up learning the trade, at least for a few years. It's funny, he's been asking me since I was fourteen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which would go first, the holidays or the flat?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The holidays, instantly. The flat would be a harder decision. I'd give it six months to see whether rents in the city hold up.

feel: **Frightened** and kept awake, though not panicked thanks to savings.

fieldNote: She expects to **lose the job**, so she's alarmed despite a calm tone.
Her **father's trade** is a real hands-on refuge for a few years.
Owning a **flat** makes her feel exposed rather than secure here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years is fast, but it's planning time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do this properly if we start now. I'd want my paper to report on it fairly, firm by firm, so readers know which local jobs are at risk. And I'd say training needs to be paid for by the firms that save money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Business owners still want to have lunch with someone who understands their firm, and I'd bet my next five years on being that person. The results stories go well before 2031, but the relationships might carry me there. After that, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the AI tools in the first year, because by then everyone sensible would be. I'd focus on interviews and features, the bosses and workers. I'd keep the flat and keep building savings. And I'd take an evening course in business finance, so I'm not reliant on Ines checking my numbers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but I'd feel I had a hand on the wheel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens after 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe I move into something hands-on, maybe my dad's business, which would have three more years. Or maybe I'm good enough by then that a firm hires me to explain itself to people. I really don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said firms that save money should pay for training. Isn't that a bit left-wing for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't think so. It's just sensible. If a firm saves a fortune, it's fair it helps the people it let go, and it keeps the town spending in its shops.

I'd say firms that **save money** should pay for retraining.

fieldNote: She'd bet on **relationships**, the human part of business reporting.

steps.text: Learn the newsroom AI tools in the first year
Take an evening course in business finance

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That changes the feeling a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we have time to plan and no excuse not to. I'd want the paper to run a series on which local jobs change and when. I'd keep it practical, not scary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With ten years I'd study accounting at night, because the people who read company numbers for a living will need a human to sign them off, at least for a while. My job looks about the same for the next few years. It's 2036 that's the cliff, and I'd be 37.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the paper, keep the flat, and keep overpaying the mortgage so it's small by the early 2030s. I'd start a part-time accounting qualification next year, about three years of evenings. I'd use AI tools when the desk does. And I'd review it all every couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy rather than worried. It's a long way off but it's definitely coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Isn't accounting also thinking work AGI would do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, I know. But a qualified person signing off accounts feels like something rules would protect longer. And it makes me a better business reporter in the meantime, so it's not wasted either way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you move sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the paper started running AI-written results stories. That'd be my signal to take the course more seriously.

fieldNote: Ten years makes her **own income** feel safe for now.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because I'd have a new mortgage and a job that goes almost overnight. What would help is a government plan with paid retraining for people early in their careers, and firms that save money from AI chipping in for it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe that cuts were already normal. Nobody at my paper has ever been sacked by a machine yet, but everyone has been sacked by a spreadsheet. AI just makes the spreadsheet faster.

She moves from **calm** to alarmed if AGI comes in two years, and back to uneasy with ten.
Her plans lean on **relationships with bosses** and, with time, an accounting qualification.
